## Design

### 2026-10-24 – In this session, I finished the schematic, added the footprints (except for the keypads), and imported it into the PCB editor. This is how my schematic looks right now:

**3h**

In this session, I finished the schematic, added the footprints (except for the keypads), and imported it into the PCB editor. This is how my schematic looks right now:

![Screenshot 2026-10-24 at 6.06.17 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/0f0e9d4b661fbcd712359223607b032ea4f2dceb425705696deaac773f808f96.png)

Instead of going with the guide, I decided to do something a little different. I decided to add a second encoder, and use both of the encoder's switches. Since I didn't have enough room on the ESP32, I got rid of the low-profile switches and a slider. The remaining slider will be used to control the volume. For the first encoder, it will control the octaves, and the second octave will be a modulation wheel. The switches will reset the octave/mod effect. These are my footprints:

![Screenshot 2026-10-24 at 6.13.05 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/373f67d4db0adfe4cea371057a22df7983b029184e4e8ab1961257d43184c35b.png)

And finally this is how it looks like in the PCB editor (without the keys):

![Screenshot 2026-10-24 at 6.14.59 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/61388d0a4828528001e6c922482e0810183ffd3bf73c4e10d16d5baba333a6f7.png)

I spent a lot of the time on the schematic and thinking on what parts I should sacrifice for the second encoder.

### 2026-10-25 – Last session, I finished the PCB, so this session I wanted to add the software changes. The 2 changes I wanted to do was have one of my encoders change the octave, and the other add a modulation effec

**5h**

Last session, I finished the PCB, so this session I wanted to add the software changes. The 2 changes I wanted to do was have one of my encoders change the octave, and the other add a modulation effect. The other change is that I wanted the neopixels to indicate what octave the keys were in, and also flash when a key was pressed.

I started by importing the USBMIDI and Adafruit_NeoPixel libraries so my computer recognizes the ESP32-S3-Zero as a native MIDI device. I mapped the pins, using TX and RX for the second encoder so I wouldn't have to solder the tiny pads underneath the board. I also created a touchPlaying array to remember which exact note each key is playing. That way, if I shift octaves while holding down a key, the board still knows which original note to turn off when I let go.

![Screenshot 2026-10-25 at 8.41.09 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/2bdd60af1280af916eb335c0bdd81a59f98c7f6b4d19df502dfd646a2cb01124.png)

Since capacitive touch pads don't click like a normal switch, I wrote updateLEDs() to give me visual feedback. If any key is held down, the NeoPixels flash bright white so I know my tap registered. When no keys are pressed, the LEDs show my current octave (green for the default middle octave (0), cooler blues for lower octaves (-1 to -4), and warmer yellow-to-red colors for higher octaves (+1 to +4)).

![Screenshot 2026-10-25 at 8.41.00 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/8d68ca37dade49cef96b1ab9e07cf2675f0d21aee2498c49420e66905faa0838.png)

In setup(), I enabled internal pull-up resistors (INPUT_PULLUP) on the encoder pins so the board didn't need extra physical resistors on the PCB. Because bare copper pads can have slightly different capacitance depending on the environment, I had the board take 16 readings per key on boot and average them into a baseline. Calibrating on startup prevents false triggers without me having to hardcode sensitivity numbers.

![Screenshot 2026-10-25 at 8.40.50 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/1ba29286474cbd5e2196ee8c26e07548cabd8a0416b27616fcff749ca534bb0b.png)

At the top of loop(), the code reads my first encoder to shift octaves. I clamped the shift between -4 and +4 so the math stays within valid MIDI limits, and added a 50ms debounce check on the encoder's click button so pressing it resets me back to the middle octave (0).

![Screenshot 2026-10-25 at 8.40.19 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/d6c3d91abe12c4709e5128976a4aed3ed348ebdbcfab80f2c6f29fe8e15aa758.png)

Next, the code reads my second encoder, which I mapped to MIDI CC 1 (Modulation Wheel) to add vibrato or synth effects. Turning a knob by 1 step from 0 to 127 takes way too many turns, so I made each click change the value by 4 for faster scrolling. Just like the first encoder, clicking the knob down instantly resets the modulation effect back to 0.

![Screenshot 2026-10-25 at 8.40.28 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/cffee43cd4187d2f746218ab9cdd49b5d53dd9ae591176f4238a6b72eed90600.png)

Finally, the loop scans the 7 touch keys and the volume slider. A key triggers if its reading jumps 25% above its startup baseline, shifting the base note by 12 semitones per octave and clamping it to the 0–127 MIDI range. For the slider, I scaled the 12-bit analog reading (0–4095) down to a 7-bit MIDI value (0–127) for Main Volume (CC 7), and made it only send updates when the value changes by more than 1 so electrical noise doesn't spam my computer with MIDI data.

![Screenshot 2026-10-25 at 8.40.36 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/a66324ab7459921537df42ef65386390c1821ba53fad9ed93e5dca6cfa8c85c0.png)
